title: Louw v. Commissioner
subject: Individual Inventor's Trade or Business Under Section 174
summary: Louw v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1971-326, is a U.S. Tax Court decision holding that an individual inventor who never manufactures products can still deduct research and experimental expenditures under IRC § 174 if he regularly and continuously develops inventions to sell or license with a genuine profit motive, because he is already engaged in a trade or business.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background
Procedural Posture and Factual Background

In Johan A. Louw v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1971-326, 30 T.C.M. (CCH) 1421, Dec. 31,131(M) (1971), the United States Tax Court adjudicated a foundational dispute regarding the deductibility of research and experimental (R&E) expenditures under Section 174 of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC). The petitioner, Johan A. Louw—who filed a joint return with his wife and co-petitioner, Aleida G. Louw—was a mechanical engineer employed by the Townsend Company who also engaged in free-lance inventive activity in his individual capacity over several years, devoting evenings, weekends, and vacations to a "Method and Apparatus for Saline Water Conversion" (a desalination apparatus), as well as to related mechanical inventions such as a throw-away plastic paint bag and a friction welder for pipelines. For the single taxable year under examination, 1966, the petitioner claimed deductions under IRC § 174(a)(1) of $2,569 incurred in developing and patenting his desalination invention, consisting of $2,473 in patent attorney fees, $72 for technical books, and $24 for patent copies.

Throughout the period at issue, the petitioner had not yet generated any gross receipts, royalties, or commercial revenue from his inventive efforts. Furthermore, the court found that the petitioner never had an expectation of manufacturing or producing the desalination apparatuses, each of which would cost several hundred thousand dollars to build. Instead, his sole commercial objective was to monetize the resulting intellectual property by selling, leasing, or licensing the patents and technical designs to third-party commercial enterprises.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

Upon examination, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue disallowed the petitioner's claimed R&E deductions in their entirety. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) predicated its challenge on a single, narrow, factual ground—the alleged absence of a trade or business nexus—and did not deny that the petitioner made the disputed outlays, that the outlays constituted research or experimental expenditures within the meaning of IRC § 174, or that the requisite election had been made. Specifically, the Commissioner determined that the expenditures, the disallowance of which produced a deficiency of $573.50 for 1966, were not paid or incurred "in connection with his trade or business" within the meaning of IRC § 174(a)(1). Relying on John F. Koons, 35 T.C. 1092 (1961), the Commissioner maintained that the petitioner was merely preparing to enter a business that would commercially exploit his patent, so that the costs of developing the patent were not currently deductible.

Although substantiation and contemporaneous documentation were not at issue in Louw itself, they form a separate and increasingly important line of IRS enforcement in later R&D tax disputes. Across later federal R&D tax jurisprudence that cites Louw, the IRS systematically challenges individual inventors, start-up ventures, and research-funding entities when their recordkeeping fails to corroborate their operational claims. In those later cases, when a taxpayer lacks commercial sales to objectively demonstrate a trade or business, the tax authority scrutinizes any absence of contemporaneous time logs, project accounting records, and technical documentation needed to establish that the research activities were conducted with continuity and regularity rather than sporadically as a hobby, as well as to verify the precise quantum of qualified research expenses (QREs).
Governing Statutory Framework

The dispute in Louw v. Commissioner was decided solely under IRC § 174 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 as in effect for 1966, but its reasoning now sits at the intersection of the federal statutory regime governing research expenditures and tax credits under the Internal Revenue Code, anchored primarily by IRC § 174, IRC § 162, and IRC § 41 (the last of which was enacted a decade after the decision). Under the statutory framework of IRC § 174(a)(1), a taxpayer is permitted to treat research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred during the taxable year "in connection with his trade or business" as expenses not chargeable to a capital account. Historically allowing an immediate deduction—and in the modern era governing the threshold definition of specified research or experimental expenditures subject to capitalization and amortization or domestic expensing—IRC § 174 serves as a critical statutory exception to the general rule that pre-operating or start-up costs must be capitalized when a taxpayer is not yet actively carrying on a business. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a), qualifying expenditures must represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense, aimed at eliminating uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product or process. Furthermore, under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(3), research costs incurred in connection with the construction or manufacture of depreciable property by another are eligible only if made "upon the taxpayer's order and at his risk".

This framework interacts closely with IRC § 162(a), which permits the deduction of ordinary and necessary expenses paid or incurred in "carrying on any trade or business". While the United States Supreme Court in Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500 (1974), subsequently confirmed that the "in connection with" standard of IRC § 174 is broader and less restrictive than the "carrying on" standard of IRC § 162(a), determining whether a taxpayer's activities rise to the level of a bona fide "trade or business" under IRC § 174 still incorporates the foundational profit motive, continuity, and regularity criteria developed under IRC § 162.

Originally enacted as IRC § 44F and subsequently recodified as IRC § 41, the federal credit for increasing research activities directly incorporates IRC § 174 as its foundational threshold. Under the four-part statutory test of IRC § 41(d)(1), "qualified research" requires first that the expenditures qualify as expenses under IRC § 174 (the Section 174 Test), second that the research be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature (the Technological Information Test), third that the application of such information be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer (the Business Component Test), and fourth that substantially all of the activities constitute elements of a process of experimentation (the Process of Experimentation Test). Crucially, under IRC § 41(b)(1), Qualified Research Expenses—comprising in-house wages, supplies, and 65% of eligible contract research expenses—are creditable only if paid or incurred by the taxpayer "in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer," while IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) expressly excludes any research funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity.
The Court's Final Holding

In Louw v. Commissioner, the United States Tax Court rejected the Commissioner's narrow construction of IRC § 174, holding that a taxpayer is not required to manufacture or produce physical goods in order to satisfy the "in connection with a trade or business" requirement. Relying on Harold T. Avery, 47 B.T.A. 538 (1942), the Tax Court established the enduring legal principle that the exploitation of inventions through royalties, sales of patents, or otherwise may constitute a valid trade or business under IRC § 174, provided the taxpayer demonstrates a genuine intention and expectation of making a profit and conducts the freelance inventive activities in a sufficiently sustained, regular, and continuous manner. Finding that the petitioner devoted his time regularly and continuously to freelance inventing over several years—an average of 25 hours per week from 1965 through 1967 and 5 to 10 hours per week during 1968 and 1969—and that he sought to market his inventions both directly to prospective manufacturers and through a patent search service, the court, while acknowledging that the evidence "may not be as strong here as in some cases," concluded that he was "not merely preparing to enter a business; he is already engaged in it".

However, Louw itself did not turn on substantiation: the Commissioner did not dispute the amount or character of the outlays, and the court made its findings regarding the petitioner's weekly hours without reference to contemporaneous time logs; the strict evidentiary boundary separating a legitimate research business from a disallowed hobby, passive investment, or unsubstantiated claim has instead been delineated by later federal R&D tax decisions that apply or distinguish Louw. Where taxpayers rely on the Louw licensing paradigm or claim R&D tax benefits under IRC §§ 174 and 41 without rigorous contemporaneous time documentation, clear separation of experimental costs from personal or routine expenses, active operational control, and documented technical experimentation, federal courts deny the claimed R&D deductions and credits in full.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

A comprehensive examination of the federal Tax Court and appellate decisions that followed and applied the Louw v. Commissioner framework—in which, unlike in Louw itself, the taxpayers frequently lost—reveals five core legal, technical, contractual, and evidentiary deficiencies that trigger IRS disallowance of R&D deductions and credits.
Failure of Contemporaneous Time Documentation and Expense Substantiation

The single most pervasive cause of total disallowance in federal R&D tax controversies involving individual inventors, closely held enterprises, and technical executives is the failure to maintain contemporaneous time and accounting records. This evidentiary deficiency operates across two distinct statutory dimensions, beginning with the burden of proving continuity and regularity to overcome hobby disqualification. Under the legal standard articulated in Louw, an inventor who has generated zero commercial revenue can qualify as a trade or business under IRC § 174 only by proving that his inventive efforts were of a "sufficiently sustained character" and constituted "regular, continuous, and extensive activity," pursued with the intention and expectation of making a profit. When a taxpayer fails to maintain contemporaneous daily or weekly time logs, laboratory notebooks, and project calendars, the taxpayer may be unable to establish the quantum of time devoted to the research venture, although in Louw itself the court made findings on the petitioner's weekly hours without reference to any such records. As demonstrated in McMullen / Everson v. Commissioner, T.C. Summary Opinion 2001-87 (a nonprecedential summary opinion citing Louw v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1971-326), when a petitioner fails to establish that he was actively engaged in research and development or in manufacturing and marketing during the taxable year, the Tax Court holds that the activity was not a trade or business for that year, resulting in a complete disallowance under IRC §§ 162 and 174.

The second dimension of this failure involves substantiating Qualified Research Expenses under IRC § 6001 and the judicial erosion of the Cohan estimation doctrine. Under IRC § 6001 and the regulations thereunder, taxpayers bear the strict legal burden of maintaining permanent books of account or records sufficient to establish the exact amount of deductions and credits claimed on a federal tax return. While federal courts historically invoked Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930), to estimate deductible expenses when a taxpayer established that qualifying activities occurred but lacked exact documentation, modern Tax Court jurisprudence under IRC § 41—including Eustace v. Commissioner, Lala v. Commissioner, Machise v. Commissioner, Redelsheimer v. Commissioner, and Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner—refuses to apply the Cohan doctrine unless the taxpayer provides a credible, contemporaneous evidentiary foundation tying specific employee hours and supply costs directly to qualified research projects. Retroactive, post-hoc time reconstructions or blanket percentage allocations of executive and engineering wages are summarily rejected by the Tax Court.
The Realistic Prospect and Passive Investor Trap in Licensing and Joint Venture Structures

While Louw established that a taxpayer need not manufacture products and may operate a trade or business exclusively by selling, leasing, or licensing patents, this exact business model triggered decades of aggressive tax structuring that the IRS and federal courts systematically dismantled. Following Louw and Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500 (1974), numerous partnerships, joint ventures, and holding entities attempted to claim IRC § 174 deductions and IRC § 41 credits by funding third-party research and claiming they were in the "trade or business of licensing" the resulting technology. In landmark decisions such as Green v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. 667 (1984), Harris v. Commissioner, 16 F.3d 75 (5th Cir. 1994), and I-Tech Ltd. Research Partnership v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2001-10, taxpayers explicitly cited Louw v. Commissioner to argue that holding and licensing technology developed by a contractor satisfied the trade or business requirement.

The federal courts rejected these claims by exposing fatal structural and contractual flaws regarding the delegation of operational control. Although Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(2) permits another entity to perform research on behalf of the taxpayer, the regulation does not permit another entity to conduct the trade or business on behalf of the taxpayer. In Louw, the taxpayer personally conducted his inventive work on a regular and continuous basis and personally sought to market his inventions—directly to prospective manufacturers such as Townsend Company and Fluor Corporation and through a patent search service—although he had not yet concluded any sale or license. Conversely, when a taxpayer contracts out both the R&D execution and the subsequent marketing or licensing activities to a research contractor, the nexus of the trade or business belongs to the contractor rather than the taxpayer.

Furthermore, judicial decisions after Snow require pre-revenue taxpayers to demonstrate a "realistic prospect" of subsequently entering into their own active trade or business utilizing the fruits of the research. Establishing a realistic prospect requires proving both an objective intent to enter the business and the operational capability of doing so, as the mere legal possibility of entering a business fails to satisfy IRC § 174. When a research contractor or an affiliate holds an option to acquire an exclusive license or purchase the resulting technology for a nominal or pre-determined fee, or where the taxpayer owns only component designs that possess no independent market value apart from the contractor's proprietary system, the taxpayer has no realistic prospect of exploiting the technology in its own business. Under these circumstances, the court recharacterizes the taxpayer as a passive investor providing financial capital rather than an active participant in a trade or business, disallowing all claimed IRC § 174 deductions and IRC § 41 credits.
The Statutory "Carrying On" Discrepancy Between IRC Section 174 and IRC Section 41

A critical statutory trap arising from reliance on Louw and Snow involves the divergent statutory language governing R&E deductions under IRC § 174 versus the R&D tax credit under IRC § 41. Under IRC § 174(a)(1), expenditures are eligible if incurred "in connection with" a taxpayer's trade or business, which allows pre-operating start-up ventures with a realistic prospect of future commercialization to qualify for section 174 treatment. In stark contrast, IRC § 41(b)(1) restricts the R&D tax credit to Qualified Research Expenses paid or incurred by the taxpayer "in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer".

Consequently, even if a taxpayer satisfies the Snow test by showing a future realistic prospect of entering a business, the taxpayer is completely disqualified from claiming the IRC § 41 R&D credit unless the taxpayer is already actively carrying on a trade or business during the taxable year in which the QREs are incurred. In Louw—decided under IRC § 174 alone, before Snow and a decade before the research credit was enacted—the Tax Court ruled in favor of the petitioner on the trade or business issue by finding as a matter of fact that because his freelance inventive activities were sustained over several years and pursued in a business-like manner with a profit motive, he was "not merely preparing to enter a business; he is already engaged in it". Taxpayers who fail to establish that their licensing or product development operations have crossed the threshold from pre-business preparation into an ongoing, active business at the time expenses are incurred forfeit the IRC § 41 credit entirely.
Failure to Prove Technological Uncertainty and a Structured Process of Experimentation

Beyond the threshold trade or business nexus, claims involving product design, software development, and engineering regularly fail due to an inability to substantiate the technical criteria of Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2 and the four-part test of IRC § 41(d)(1). As reflected in the federal case law matrix surrounding Louw—including Best Lock Corp. v. Commissioner, Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, Harris v. Commissioner, and Black & Decker Corp. v. Commissioner—taxpayers frequently conflate routine engineering with genuine technological uncertainty. Under IRC § 174, Rev. Proc. 69-21, and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2, research costs qualify only where the operational feasibility, capability, method, or appropriate design of the product or software is seriously in doubt at the outset of the project. Routine manufacturing adjustments, aesthetic product fit-testing, and routine software conversions or configurations do not resolve genuine technological uncertainty and are strictly disqualified; by contrast, the costs of obtaining a patent, such as attorneys' fees for making and perfecting a patent application, are expressly included in R&E expenditures under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1)—and the Commissioner in Louw did not dispute that the petitioner's $2,473 in patent attorney fees qualified—although such legal fees do not constitute qualified research expenses for purposes of the IRC § 41 credit.

Additionally, under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), substantially all—defined by regulation as at least 80%—of the research activities with respect to a business component must constitute elements of a structured process of experimentation. Taxpayers must prove through contemporaneous technical records that they identified specific technical uncertainties grounded in the hard sciences, formulated scientific or engineering hypotheses, designed and conducted systematic modeling, simulation, or trial-and-error testing of alternatives, and evaluated the resulting empirical data to refine or discard hypotheses. Undocumented tinkering by an individual inventor or ad-hoc trial-and-error lacking structured hypothesis evaluation fails this statutory mandate. Similarly, where taxpayers claim substantial supply expenses for fabricating prototypes or pilot models, failure to prove that the physical model was constructed solely to resolve technical design uncertainties—or failure to evaluate substantially all elements of the pilot model vessel or apparatus in a process of experimentation—results in the complete disallowance of claimed supply QREs.
Contractual Failures: Funded Research Exclusions and Financial Risk

When research and development involves third-party contracts—whether an inventor licensing designs to a corporate sponsor or an enterprise hiring an outside engineering contractor—contractual drafting failures frequently destroy credit eligibility under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(3). To avoid the funded research exclusion under IRC § 41 and satisfy the "at his risk" mandate under IRC § 174, two strict contractual prongs must be satisfied under governing federal precedent, including Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner, and Grigsby v. United States.

First, the taxpayer claiming the R&D tax credit must bear the financial risk of technical failure through explicit payment contingency. If an engineering firm or inventor performs research under a fixed-fee or cost-plus contract where payment is guaranteed regardless of technical success, or if a sponsor reimburses the researcher's costs without contingency, the research is deemed funded and disqualified. Conversely, if a taxpayer pays a third-party contractor to develop technology, the contract must explicitly stipulate that the contractor does not guarantee technical success and that the expenditures are incurred solely upon the taxpayer's order and at the taxpayer's financial risk. Second, under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), a taxpayer cannot claim the R&D credit if it retains "no substantial rights" in the research results. If a contract transfers exclusive ownership of all resulting patents, designs, and know-how to a client or corporate partner without reserving to the researcher the right to use the technology in its own business without paying a royalty, the researcher fails the substantial rights test and forfeits the credit.
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement implicated in Louw v. Commissioner and related federal R&D tax jurisprudence against the specific taxpayer failures that trigger IRS disallowance and the corresponding judicial standard of proof required by the United States Tax Court and federal appellate courts.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how taxpayers and technical tax counsel must operationalize the legal holdings of Louw v. Commissioner and related federal IRC §§ 174 and 41 precedent, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic commercial ventures facing the exact statutory and evidentiary pitfalls identified in the ruling, accompanied by step-by-step remedial restructuring protocols.
Case Study 1: Pre-Revenue Clean-Tech Desalination and Membrane IP Licensing Venture
Baseline Scenario and Legal Pitfalls

AquaFlux Innovations LLC ("AquaFlux"), a domestic limited liability company taxed as a partnership, was founded by a principal chemical engineer and backed by four individual members. Echoing the technical domain of Johan A. Louw, AquaFlux was formed to develop a novel, low-energy forward-osmosis desalination membrane and multi-stage brine recovery apparatus. AquaFlux owns no manufacturing plants and never intends to manufacture desalination equipment; its business model is strictly to patent the membrane architecture and license the intellectual property to municipal water treatment original equipment manufacturers (OEMs).

During Year 1 and Year 2, AquaFlux generated zero gross revenue and encountered three severe legal vulnerabilities that threaten complete disallowance under IRS examination. First, although the principal engineer worked full-time on the membrane design while drawing compensation, and two other technical members contributed part-time engineering support, none of the personnel maintained contemporaneous time logs. At year-end, the company's accountant allocated 100% of compensation and laboratory lease costs to IRC § 174 R&E deductions and IRC § 41 QREs based solely on uncorroborated oral estimates. Second, because AquaFlux had no active licensing agreements, no marketing infrastructure, and no ongoing commercial operations, an IRS examiner can assert that while AquaFlux might be preparing to enter a business, it was not actively "carrying on" a trade or business as required to claim the R&D credit under IRC § 41(b)(1). Third, to test the high-pressure fluid dynamics of the membrane, AquaFlux contracted with HydroTech Corp., an established water treatment manufacturer, paying HydroTech $450,000. Under the research agreement, HydroTech performed the laboratory testing, and AquaFlux granted HydroTech an exclusive option to acquire the worldwide patent rights to the membrane for a pre-set flat fee of $50,000 upon completion of testing. Under Green and Harris, this nominal option strips AquaFlux of any "realistic prospect" of operating its own licensing business, converting AquaFlux into a passive investor funding HydroTech's business. Compounding this error, AquaFlux included $40,000 of patent attorney filing fees within its claimed IRC § 41 QRE pool.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Establishing an Active Trade or Business

To satisfy both the "in connection with" standard of IRC § 174 under Louw and the stricter "carrying on" mandate of IRC § 41(b)(1), AquaFlux must immediately formalize its active intellectual property licensing operations. Under Louw v. Commissioner and the authority on which it relied, Harold T. Avery, 47 B.T.A. 538 (1942), exploiting inventions through royalties and patent licensing may constitute a trade or business when conducted with continuity, regularity, and a genuine intention and expectation of making a profit. AquaFlux must establish dedicated commercial licensing governance by adopting a formal IP Commercialization Charter, maintaining dedicated laboratory and administrative records, registering as a commercial technology vendor with municipal water authorities, and executing Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs) and Joint Evaluation Letters of Intent with multiple prospective OEM licensees to establish a prospective revenue stream from multiple sources rather than a single captive party.

Furthermore, if AquaFlux has not yet commenced active licensing operations sufficient to independently satisfy the "carrying on" threshold of IRC § 41(b)(1), AquaFlux should form an operating joint venture—structured as a general partnership or operating LLC—with an established commercial enterprise that contributes an ongoing business function, such as an active water-treatment engineering consulting or marketing division. As established in federal R&D structuring doctrine, when the joint venture is actively carrying on a trade or business under IRC § 162 during the research period and contracts for research on its own behalf and at its own risk, the venture satisfies the statutory trade or business prerequisite to qualify for the research and development tax credit under IRC § 41.
Step 2: Reforming Contract Terms to Eliminate the Passive Investor and Funded Research Traps

AquaFlux must immediately amend its agreement with HydroTech Corp. to comply with Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(3), IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), and the judicial standards of Harris and Grigsby (Louw itself involved no contract research arrangement). First, AquaFlux must revoke the pre-wired $50,000 flat-fee exclusive purchase option granted to HydroTech. If HydroTech desires an option to license or purchase the resulting technology, the option must be exercisable only at fair market value determined after the research period concludes, or structured as a non-exclusive, market-rate royalty license negotiated at arm's length, ensuring AquaFlux retains full legal and economic ownership of the patents and a realistic prospect of commercially exploiting the technology.

Second, the contract research agreement with HydroTech must incorporate explicit "order and risk" provisions pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(3) and the funded-research rules of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d). The contract must state that HydroTech is performing specific fluid-dynamic testing services solely upon AquaFlux's order and at AquaFlux's financial risk, that HydroTech does not guarantee the technical success or operational feasibility of the membrane, and that AquaFlux bears 100% of the financial loss if the membrane fails to achieve target osmotic flux rates. Finally, the agreement must vest 100% of all right, title, and interest in the resulting inventions, test data, and know-how exclusively in AquaFlux, thereby preserving AquaFlux's substantial rights and securing its eligibility to claim 65% of the HydroTech payments as contract research QREs under IRC § 41(b)(3).
Step 3: Overhauling Technical Documentation to Prove Uncertainty and Experimentation

To prevent the IRS from disqualifying the membrane development as routine engineering or unsubstantiated tinkering, AquaFlux must implement a stage-gate technical documentation protocol. Prior to commencing each phase of membrane synthesis, the principal engineer must author a contemporaneous Project Initiation Technical Brief documenting why standard reverse-osmosis membranes cannot achieve the target desalination recovery rate—such as exceeding 85% recovery at less than a specified maximum hydraulic pressure—using known engineering methods, explicitly establishing capability and appropriate design uncertainty under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a). Simultaneously, in accordance with Best Lock Corp. v. Commissioner, AquaFlux must strictly segregate the $40,000 in patent attorney legal and filing fees from its IRC § 41 QRE calculation, as legal costs of perfecting a patent application are not wages, supplies, or contract research expenses eligible for the R&D tax credit—although, as Louw illustrates and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) expressly provides, such patent costs remain research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174.
Step 4: Implementing Contemporaneous Time and Experimentation Tracking

To directly address the time-documentation disallowance risk illustrated by Everson / McMullen and later R&D credit decisions (a risk not presented in Louw, where substantiation was uncontested), AquaFlux must deploy a mandatory digital time-tracking protocol requiring the principal engineer and all technical personnel to log hours daily by specific project code and activity category. The system must segregate hours into direct experimental design and hypothesis formulation, direct laboratory testing and prototype fabrication, direct supervision of HydroTech contract testing, non-qualifying patent legal coordination, and commercial licensing and marketing activities. While commercial licensing hours are excluded from the IRC § 41 QRE numerator, contemporaneous logs of those licensing activities provide vital objective evidence that AquaFlux is actively engaged in the trade or business of licensing under Louw. Furthermore, every laboratory run must be recorded in a timestamped Electronic Lab Notebook (ELN) mapping each time entry to a documented scientific hypothesis, an experimental test protocol, empirical test data measuring permeate flux in liters per square meter per hour (LMH) and salt rejection percentages, and a technical evaluation conclusion.
Case Study 2: Custom Industrial Automation and Embedded Software Engineering Firm
Baseline Scenario and Legal Pitfalls

Vanguard Mechatronics Inc. ("Vanguard"), a domestic C-corporation, designs and builds custom automated robotic assembly lines and embedded machine-vision control software for aerospace and food-processing manufacturers. During the tax year, Vanguard claimed $1.2 million in federal R&D tax credits under IRC § 41 across two major initiatives: Project A, which involved developing a custom high-speed vision-guided robotic sorting system for an external food-processing client, and Project B, which involved developing an internal enterprise software module to manage its own shop-floor inventory and project scheduling.

Upon audit review, Vanguard's claim exhibits three severe legal and evidentiary defects. First, under Project A, Vanguard executed a Master Services Agreement (MSA) with its client under a fixed-price contract of $4.5 million. The contract paid Vanguard in monthly progress installments based on calendar milestones rather than technical acceptance criteria, contained no provision requiring Vanguard to refund progress payments if the robotic system failed to meet throughput specifications, and stipulated that all custom designs and software created under the Statement of Work would become the sole property of the client. Under Fairchild Industries, Grigsby, and fixed-fee engineering case law, Project A is disqualified as "funded research" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) because Vanguard lacked specific financial risk on the progress payments and failed to retain substantial rights in the resulting designs. Second, Vanguard included $1.8 million of structural steel framing, standard servo motors, and commercial conveyor hardware in its IRC § 41(b)(2) supply QREs, claiming the entire production line delivered to the client was a "pilot model," without proving that substantially all elements of the line were technically uncertain or evaluated in a process of experimentation. Third, under Project B, Vanguard modified an off-the-shelf software package for internal use and included 50% of its Chief Executive Officer's and Vice President of Engineering's W-2 wages ($400,000) in QREs based on year-end executive interviews, with zero contemporaneous time logs or commit records proving direct supervision or direct performance of qualified research. Under Eustace and Redelsheimer (rather than Louw, which involved no substantiation dispute), the unsubstantiated executive wages and routine off-the-shelf software modifications face complete disallowance.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Reforming Commercial Contracts to Satisfy Financial Risk and Substantial Rights

To rescue custom engineering projects like Project A from the funded research exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), Vanguard must redraft its standard MSA and Statements of Work in accordance with Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States so that all milestone payments are expressly contingent upon the successful completion of formal technical acceptance testing, such as Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT) and Site Acceptance Testing (SAT) verifying micron-level accuracy and cycle-time thresholds. The contract must explicitly stipulate that any interim progress advances are refundable deposits until the client executes a formal Certificate of Technical Acceptance, and that Vanguard bears the full financial obligation to redesign, rework, or refund all payments at its own expense if the system fails to achieve the specified technical performance parameters.

Simultaneously, following Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner, Vanguard must modify its intellectual property clauses to distinguish between client-specific physical deliverables and Vanguard's underlying engineering designs, algorithms, and know-how. The contract must explicitly reserve to Vanguard ownership of all underlying patents, source code libraries, kinematics algorithms, and engineering drawings—granting the client a license to operate the delivered machine—or reserve to Vanguard a perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free right to use all designs, technological information, and know-how developed during the project in Vanguard's future business operations without paying any fee or royalty to the client, thereby satisfying the substantial rights mandate.
Step 2: Restructuring Pilot Model Governance and Supply Accounting

To overcome the pilot model and supply substantiation failures identified in Black & Decker, Trinity Industries, and Little Sandy Coal, Vanguard must cease claiming entire commercial assembly lines as single pilot models where routine structural steel and off-the-shelf conveyors dilute the "substantially all" 80% experimentation threshold. Instead, Vanguard must apply the shrinking-back rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) at the project governance level, defining the specific technically uncertain sub-assemblies—such as the End-of-Arm Pneumatic Gripper Mechanism and the Sub-Millisecond Optical Sensor Array—as distinct business components. Vanguard must establish segregated general ledger job-costing work orders solely for the experimental fabrication and testing of those specific sub-assembly prototypes prior to commercial manufacturing, ensuring that only materials consumed in resolving genuine design uncertainty are coded to the IRC § 41 supply QRE account.
Step 3: Applying the High Threshold of Innovation Test to Internal-Use Software

To prevent audit disallowance on Project B under the internal-use software (IUS) transition and regulatory rules applied in Eustace v. Commissioner and FedEx Corp., Vanguard must conduct a rigorous technical review and remove all costs associated with installing, configuring, migrating data, or routine scripting of the commercial off-the-shelf ERP software, as such activities fail both the general four-part test and the high threshold of innovation requirements. Only if Project B contains a custom-coded software module that either interfaces directly with third-party shop-floor robotics hardware as operational embedded software or independently satisfies the three-part High Threshold of Innovation Test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)—proving that the software is innovative in achieving a substantial and economically significant reduction in cost or improvement in speed, involves significant economic risk where technical uncertainty prevents a guarantee of capital recovery within a reasonable period, and is not commercially available for purchase, lease, or license without fundamental modifications—should Vanguard isolate that module into a dedicated R&D project code supported by architectural uncertainty documentation.
Step 4: Enforcing Strict Contemporaneous Time Substantiation for Engineers and Executives

To eliminate the documentation failures highlighted in later substantiation and executive wage disallowance rulings such as Redelsheimer (failures that were not at issue in Louw v. Commissioner), Vanguard must terminate the practice of relying on year-end percentage estimates. All mechanical, electrical, and software engineers must log hours weekly into an ERP timekeeping system tied directly to specific sub-component project codes and version-control commit tickets. Furthermore, because IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) limits qualified services to engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research, and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c) confines "direct supervision" to first-line supervision rather than higher-level general management, the Vice President of Engineering must maintain a contemporaneous calendar log, sign off on technical finite-element-analysis (FEA) design review minutes, and record exact hours spent in hands-on technical troubleshooting sessions with lead engineers, while excluding all unlogged general management hours of the CEO and VP from the QRE calculation.
Summary Matrix of Remedial Governance and Compliance Protocols
The table below synthesizes the operational, contractual, and evidentiary transformations required across both case studies to achieve full statutory compliance under IRC §§ 174 and 41.

cells: Entity & Commercial Structure (Case Study 1)
Zero revenue with uncorroborated licensing intent; lack of active "carrying on" status for IRC § 41 credits.
Formalize multi-party OEM licensing outreach, NDAs, and commercialization charter, or form an active operating Joint Venture with an ongoing business partner.
IRC § 174(a)(1); IRC § 41(b)(1); Louw v. Commissioner; Harold T. Avery
Outbound Contract R&D & Options (Case Study 1)
Granting contractor a $50,000 flat-fee exclusive purchase option, reducing taxpayer to a passive investor.
Revoke nominal purchase option; require fair-market-value post-R&D licensing terms; insert explicit "upon taxpayer's order and at its financial risk" clauses.
Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(3); Green v. Commissioner; Harris v. Commissioner
Inbound Customer Contracts (Case Study 2)
Fixed-price progress payments without technical contingency and complete forfeiture of IP ownership ("funded research").
Tie all milestone payments to formal FAT/SAT technical acceptance criteria with refund/rework risk; reserve perpetual royalty-free rights to underlying designs and know-how.
IRC § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d); Fairchild Industries; Populous Holdings; Grigsby
Prototype Supplies & IUS Software (Case Studies 1 & 2)
Inclusion of patent attorney filing fees in § 41 QREs, entire commercial assembly lines as pilot models, and routine COTS software modifications.

Exclude patent legal fees from § 41 QREs (while retaining them as § 174 expenditures under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1)); disaggregate uncertain sub-assemblies via "shrinking-back" job orders; isolate software meeting the High Threshold of Innovation Test.
IRC § 41(d)(1); Best Lock Corp.; Black & Decker; Eustace v. Commissioner
Time & Experimentation Tracking (Case Studies 1 & 2)
Retroactive oral estimates of engineer and executive wages; lack of structured hypothesis testing logs.
Enforce daily/weekly project-code time tracking integrated with ELN/Git test logs; substantiate executive "direct supervision" via signed technical review minutes.
IRC § 6001; Everson / McMullen; Redelsheimer; Louw v. Commissioner (contrast only—substantiation not contested)

body.text: Conclusion

The United States Tax Court's ruling in Louw v. Commissioner remains a cornerstone of federal research and development tax jurisprudence under IRC § 174—the only provision it construed—and, through § 174's role as the threshold test for the later-enacted IRC § 41 credit, it informs credit analysis as well. While the decision established the vital doctrinal rule that an inventor need not manufacture physical products and may satisfy the statutory trade or business requirement through the regular, continuous making of inventions for sale, lease, or licensing to others, subsequent judicial history demonstrates that this substantive flexibility is paired with unforgiving evidentiary and structural rigor. To withstand IRS scrutiny and prevail before the Tax Court, taxpayers must pair active operational control over their research and commercialization activities with ironclad contractual risk allocation, segregated sub-component accounting, documented scientific experimentation, and strictly contemporaneous time substantiation.

metaDescription: Louw v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1971-326: an inventor who never manufactures can deduct IRC § 174 costs if he develops inventions to sell or license.
